newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks seen squeezed out of overseas funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks seen squeezed out of overseas funds.

text.p: The recent erosion of Tokyo stock prices could spell trouble for Japanese banks in meeting global standards for raising funds overseas, analysts say.

Banking sources said that if the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares were to fall to around the 15,000-point level by the time banks close their books at the end of March, their hidden profits on shareholdings would be wiped out, seriously hurting their earnings and ability to write off bad debts.
The banks would then face difficulties meeting global capital requirements as they rely heavily on equity investment for capital and capital would be eaten up to cover losses.
The Tokyo stock market has plunged more than 15 percent since early December. The Nikkei 225 hit 17,303.65 points on January 10, its lowest close since August 1995.

Some analysts say a fall to the 15,000 level by the end of March remains a possibility and even at current levels, banks may be obliged to take steps to boost their capitalisation to remain competitive in overseas business.

"What Japanese banks have been doing is to write off bad loans to increase their credit ratings. But if the Tokyo stock market collapses, some of them may end up being trapped in a vicious circle," said Shin Nagai, money market manager of the Treasury Department at ABN AMRO Bank's Tokyo branch.
"They might not even meet BIS ratio requirements."
Under rules set out by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), banks operating globally must have a capital adequacy ratio of more than eight percent of its capital to its risk-related assets.
If a bank's ratio were to fall below eight percent, it would face difficulties raising funds overseas.

Japan's 20 major banks enjoyed a ratio of 9.34 percent on average at the end of September. But if the Nikkei remains at current levels through March 31, this could fall to just over eight percent by the fiscal year-end.

The slump in stocks has already increased the cost of fundraising overseas for Japanese banks, called the "Japan premium". On Tuesday, Japanese banks were paying an average premium of 15 basis points in the three-month Eurodollar deposit market, money traders said.

"Suppose the Tokyo stock market ended on March 31 at the current price level, the total capital of Japan's major 20 banks would decline by about 1 trillion yen ($8.4 billion) due to narrowing unrealised profits on stocks," said Akira Takai, banking industry analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research.
"The banks are very likely to finance that by issuing subordinated debts in order to keep the BIS ratio above their target level of nine percent," he said.
Bankers and analysts said that there were two ways for banks to keep their BIS ratios from falling if the unrealised profits on their stock holdings were to plummet.
One was to avoid going into the red at the fiscal year-end by passing on the writing off of bad loans, and the other was to raise capital by issuing stocks or subordinated debt.

However, issuing preferred stocks would further hurt the stock market and not all banks can afford to issue subordinated bonds overseas, though some may be able to take out the loans at home, analysts said.
Analysts said banks are hesitant to cut lending, as Japan's slow economic recovery has already dampened total domestic lending volume, and they are afraid of losing market share.
The Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd is one of the few banks to say it will cut lending to improve operational efficiency.
"It is not easy at the moment for any bank to raise capital by increasing profits or by issuing stocks. So we have decided to review the profitability of some loans," a spokesman said.

One senior official at a major Japanese bank, who asked not to be identified, said that even if hidden stock profits fell to nil, his bank would manage to keep its BIS ratio just above eight percent without extra measures.
"But we do hope to do something to raise the ratio further from that level of just above eight percent," he said.
